prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

I hold two fingers to my head, trigger my thumb, I say pow. I slice my throat with a single stroke, pull an invisible blade vertically along my vein. Remember the deaths we did together? Twiddling oven knobs in the air then thrusting our chins to inhale? I loved you so much during that experimental play when you slowly leant forward to nick your femoral artery then quietly bled out in your seat until curtain call, blood only we saw. As well as death, we’d mime marriage. I’d slide on a spectral ring and you’d shiver at the thrill of my thumb and fingertip sealing the deal for a second till the thought melted back into your skin. I am proficient at beginnings, the Air Year: the anniversary prior to paper for which ephemeral gifts are traditional. Only after our rings became solid silver did they truly disappear. Now the house is a mime scene. Mime blood all over the floor, trodden into carpet fibers, shirts, bras, dried to an airy crust under my nails. I slit my neck at the traffic lights, pow on the train, I suspend my non-knife above my head, “see what you’re making me do.” Red whirls rise from the cuts. All these huge thoughts come to nothing. My shadow is the chalk outline of a woman who did not jump.

# The Air Year

We had a ritual, my partner and I, one that belonged to no one but us. We mimed our deaths together. In the privacy of our shared world, we would enact these small suicides—a hand pressed to the temple, a slow collapse, a final breath released—and they became sacred precisely because no one else could witness them. These were performances staged for an audience of two, deaths rehearsed not out of despair but out of intimacy. To die in front of another person, even in mime, was to trust them completely.

Alongside these deaths, we married each other endlessly. We exchanged invisible rings, slipping nothing onto each other's fingers with all the ceremony the gesture deserved. These were ephemeral vows, connections made of air and gesture, dissolving the moment they were made. There was something honest in their impermanence. We were, I think, very good at beginnings. We celebrated what we called our "Air Year" anniversary, an occasion marked by imaginary gifts—temporary offerings that existed only in the moment of their giving, then vanished, leaving nothing behind but the memory of having given.

Perhaps I should have understood then what we were. We were artists of the provisional, fluent in the language of things that do not last.

The trouble came when the rings turned to silver. When we made the commitment real—when we exchanged something solid, something with weight and permanence—the relationship began to fail. It seems paradoxical, but I have come to believe that in making our bond tangible, we caused it to truly vanish. The imaginary rings had held us together precisely because they asked nothing of us but the gesture. The silver ones demanded that we mean it, and in that demand, whatever we had shared dissolved. We could survive anything, it turned out, except the real.

Now I am alone, and still I mime my deaths. But the ritual has changed. What was once private has become compulsive, and I perform these enacted deaths obsessively, in public, on street corners and in crowded rooms, before strangers who cannot know what they are seeing. I am haunted by thoughts that were never finished, by words left unspoken, by the persistent sense that something essential has been lost and cannot be recovered. I keep dying, over and over, in front of everyone—and no one witnesses it at all.
outputs.L4:
# Mime

We were always miming, the two of us. I would mime the pulling of a trigger against my temple, and you would mime the tears, wiping them from your cheeks with fingers that touched nothing. This was how we spoke. This was how we loved.

You mimed a knife once. Drew it slow across your throat while I watched from the kitchen doorway, and I applauded, because what else could I do? The blade was air. The blood was air. Everything between us had become this—a theater of the invisible, where we performed our worst impulses and called it intimacy.

I mimed swallowing pills. A whole bottle, tilting back my head, my throat working around emptiness. You did not stop me. You never stopped me. You only watched with those wet-mimed eyes and let me finish the act, let me collapse onto the floor in a death that fooled no one, least of all ourselves.

We mimed a wedding. Do you remember? I mimed the slipping of a ring onto your finger, and for once the ring was solid—I felt it, cold and real, a weight that shouldn't have existed. We looked at each other, startled. Then it disappeared. The way everything disappeared. The way you disappeared, a little more each day, until I was miming a marriage to a woman who was already gone.

The mime blood came later. It seeped from under the doors, pooled in the corners, stained the ceiling of the apartment we shared. Invisible, yes, but I could see it. I was always the only one who could see it. It ran from the wounds we pretended to give each other, and it was everywhere, and no one believed me when I said the walls were weeping.

I mimed my grief at your funeral. You were not dead. You stood beside me, miming your own grief, and we grieved together for a death that had not happened, for a love that had. The mourners were air. The coffin was air. You reached for my hand and there was nothing to hold.

This is what I want you to understand. The suffering was real even when the gestures were not. The trigger, the blade, the pills—I meant them. Every ephemeral, empty motion carried the full weight of what I could not say aloud. And you knew. You always knew. You used it, the way you used everything, turning my invisible wounds into a performance you could control.

In the end, the mime blood dried. The disappearing rings stopped appearing. We stood in the ruins of all our pantomimed catastrophes, and I understood at last that nothing had happened. Nothing had ever happened. All that pain, all that private drowning—it left no mark, no body, no evidence.

Only the mime remained. Only the nothing.

Only the two of us, gesturing at each other across an empty stage, bleeding a blood that no one, no one, would ever see.
outputs.L5:
# Waiting Room

I still **remember** the afternoon we spent in that quiet waiting room, the two of us sitting side by side on stiff plastic chairs. The clock ticked slowly, and there was little to do but pass the time.

You were **twiddling** your thumbs, a nervous habit you'd had for as long as I'd known you. Round and round they went, one over the other, while your eyes darted toward the door every time it opened. I wanted to reach out and still your hands, to tell you everything would be fine, but I didn't yet know if that was true.

The **air** in the room felt heavy, thick with the anticipation of everyone waiting for news that would change their day, or perhaps their lives. A fan spun lazily overhead, stirring the stale atmosphere without really cooling anyone down. Somewhere down the hall, a phone rang and went unanswered.

When they finally called your name, you stood up quickly, and for a moment your restless hands went perfectly still. You looked at me and smiled—a small, brave smile—and I knew then that whatever happened, we would face it together.

Now, years later, I **remember** that room not for the worry it held, but for the quiet moment we shared in it. Sometimes the smallest memories, the ones filled with **twiddling** thumbs and heavy **air**, are the ones that stay with us the longest.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a piece of experimental flash fiction about a couple who mime deaths and marriage together, using the recurring image of invisible gestures becoming real. Make it dark and lyrical.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Company of Small Endings

They met performing nothing.

She was drowning at the corner of Fifth and Bleecker, hands pressed against a wall of water only she could see. He was the man who stopped, who watched her cheeks fill with air she didn't have, who cupped his palms and offered her a rope that wasn't there.

She took it. That was the first mistake, or the first vow. Later they would disagree about which.

---

**How they married:**

No officiant. Just the two of them in the empty theater after hours, exchanging rings of air. He slid nothing onto her finger and she felt the cold of it, the weight, the way metal warms to a body it intends to stay with. When she looked down her hand had learned to hold the shape. A pale band where the sun would never reach.

*You may kiss*, said no one.

They pressed their mouths toward each other and stopped an inch apart. Kissed the space. The space kissed back. When they parted her lower lip was bruised and neither of them had touched it.

---

**How they practiced dying:**

Every performance, one of them killed the other. This was the act. This was the marriage, if you want the truth of it.

Monday: she poisoned him. Lifted an empty glass to his lips, tilted it, and he tasted almonds, felt his throat close around the absence of liquid. His knees found the floor. His eyes rolled back into a genuine dark.

Tuesday: he strangled her. Hands around a throat he never gripped. But her windpipe remembered pressure. Her face went the violet of a real ending and the audience gasped and clapped and did not know they were watching something that would not fully undo itself when the lights came up.

Because here is the thing about miming death. You have to believe it to sell it. And belief, practiced nightly, leaves residue.

---

**The residue:**

She started coughing up water in her sleep. He woke to the taste of almonds he had never swallowed. The bruise on her throat came back on Wednesdays without a single hand. Their bodies were keeping ledgers of the deaths they'd only suggested.

*It's method*, he told her. *It's just how good we are.*

But she had begun to see the rope. The one from Fifth and Bleecker. It hung now in their bedroom, thick and frayed and utterly invisible except that she could see it. She could see it.

---

**What they refused to mime:**

Love. Actual love. That, they only ever did for real, clumsy and unrehearsed, no audience, no craft. And so of all the things between them, it was the only thing that never quite became solid. It stayed gesture. It stayed reaching.

The deaths grew realer. The marriage grew realer. The invisible ring cut a groove to the bone.

But love—love they performed so honestly it never learned the trick of arriving.

---

**The last performance:**

She stood at the edge of a bridge that wasn't there. He reached for her across a gap that was only floorboards, only air, only the dark breath of the house.

He offered her the rope.

This time she saw it for what it had always been. Not rescue. Tether. The thing that pulls two people down together, hand over hand, into the water they've been swallowing all along.

She took it anyway.

That was the first vow. Or the first mistake.

The audience stood. They wept for something so beautifully unreal.

And in the empty seat where no one sat, the space wept back.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short surreal prose poem in the first person about miming suicide and marriage as expressions of love in a failing relationship.
counterfactuals.output:
**Pantomime for Two**

I mimed my own death across the kitchen tile, hand to throat, the invisible rope thrown over a rafter that was never there, and you applauded from the sink where you were washing the same plate you'd washed for a decade. *Encore*, you said, so I died again, more slowly this time, clutching the air like a bouquet.

We had run out of words the way a house runs out of light—room by room, going dim.

So I proposed instead. I knelt on the linoleum and offered you a ring of steam rising off the kettle, and you slid it onto a finger it could never fit, and we were married in the language of gestures, in the church of the failing afternoon. You wept without water. I laughed without sound.

This is how we loved by then: performing the extremes we could no longer feel, the wedding and the noose, both hands miming devotion to an audience of one.

Look how I would die for you, I signed.

Look how I would stay, you signed back.

And neither of us moved, two actors in a theater where the curtain had already fallen, still bowing, still bowing, to the empty red velvet seats.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a piece of literary flash fiction narrated by a woman whose relationship is portrayed through the metaphor of mime—invisible knives, air weddings, imaginary blood staining a real house.
counterfactuals.output:
**Marcel's Wife**

He proposed with a ring I couldn't see. Knelt in the kitchen, pinched empty air between two fingers, and I held out my hand because what else do you do when a man offers you nothing so beautifully.

The wedding was all pantomime. My mother wept real tears at imaginary vows. We fed each other cake that wasn't there, and I remember how carefully he cupped his palm beneath my chin to catch the crumbs of it, as though a mess could be made from absence.

For a while, this was our happiness. He would come home and mime the pouring of wine, and I would drink until I felt it, and some nights I truly did, a warmth spreading that no bottle ever gave me. We danced to music neither of us could hear but both of us kept time to. This is the trick they don't tell you about love: how much of it is agreement. How much is two people deciding to see the same nothing.

Then came the knives.

The first one, I didn't understand. His hand drew back, thrust forward, and I felt it—here, below the ribs, a cold that had no blade. I laughed, because surely this was a new game. But he did not laugh. He pulled the invisible thing out and I felt that too, the slow withdrawal, and something began to spill.

You'd be surprised what imaginary blood will do to a real house.

It doesn't wash out. I've tried. I've knelt on actual tile with actual rags and scrubbed at stains only I can see, spreading across the grout like a map of every silence between us. He walks through it in his socks and tracks it down the hall. I find handprints on the walls at the height of an argument. The mattress is soaked through with all the nights we performed forgiveness for each other, elaborate reconciliations, hands pressed to hearts—and meant nothing, and knew it, and took our bows anyway.

My mother asks why I stay. I can't explain that you cannot leave a man over a wound that leaves no mark. I show her the kitchen floor and she sees only clean tile. *There's nothing there,* she says, and she is right, and this is the whole horror of it.

Last night he reached for me in the dark. Empty hand, offering the empty ring again, the way he does when he wants to begin the story over. And I felt the old pull to take it, to agree, to see the diamond glinting in the nothing.

Instead I mimed a suitcase.

I packed it with great care—folding clothes that weren't there, the weight of it real in my hand as I lifted it from the bed. He watched me. He understood. That was the cruelty of a man so fluent in absence: he never once pretended not to know.

At the door I performed the turning of a key. And he did the only honest thing he'd done in years.

He let me feel the cold rush of a door, opening, into air.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an intense, poetic short story about grief and a decaying marriage where the narrator constantly performs mimed self-harm gestures in public and at home. Include the idea of an "Air Year" anniversary of ephemeral gifts.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Air Year

We are married eleven years, and this is the year of air.

I read once that anniversaries have themes—paper, cotton, tin—a slow accumulation toward the golden. But somewhere in the ledger of us, the columns emptied. Now we give each other nothing you can hold. This year I gave you a held breath in the doorway. You gave me your back, turning, the particular architecture of your shoulder blades like two folded wings that would not open.

Our daughter has been dead four months.

I want to tell you what my hands do now. I did not decide it. In the grocery, between the bruised apples and the wet green mist that falls on lettuce like a small false weather, my right hand rises to my throat and draws across it—slow, theatrical, a blade that isn't there. The woman weighing onions does not see. Or she sees and looks down. My hand comes away clean. There is no red. There is only the gesture, the pantomime of an ending I keep rehearsing but cannot perform.

At home I do it at the sink. You are drying the one plate we still use. My hand lifts, mimes the pills poured into the palm, the palm to the mouth, the swallow. I make the swallow real. That part I can commit to. You watch the window instead, where the garden has gone to seed, where her swing still hangs, the seat furred with rain and lichen, moving without wind.

"Stop," you say. Not looking. You always know.

But it isn't a threat, and you know that too. It is a language. It is the only honest thing left in this house—my body speaking the grammar of what grief wants and what cowardice denies. Each mimed wound is a letter I write and do not send. *This is how much. This is the shape of it. This is what I would do if I could bear to leave you here alone inside it.*

Because that is the cruelty: I cannot even finish the sentence my hands keep starting. To finish would be to give you the widowerhood on top of the fatherless. So I stay. I mime. I press the invisible barrel to the temple in the car at red lights, and the light goes green, and I drive us home through the dissolving town.

For the Air Year I planned a gift.

I stood in her room, which we do not enter, which we have preserved like a wound kept from healing so it cannot scar. I opened the window. I let the cold pour in over the small bed, the stuffed grey rabbit with its one loved-off ear. I cupped my hands and I caught the air that had touched her things—the last air, I told myself, that still remembered the weight of her—and I carried it down the stairs in the bowl of my palms.

You were at the table. Eleven years thinner than the man I married, your face a landscape after a long drought.

I opened my hands over yours.

"For the anniversary," I said. "Air."

And you—my love, my ruin, my fellow prisoner—you closed your fingers around nothing as though it were everything. You held our daughter's last breath, the invented relic, the ephemeral gift that would evaporate before we finished grieving it. Your knuckles whitened. A sound came out of you I had not heard since the hospital, since the machine's flat green line, since the world tipped and spilled her out of it.

And I understood then what my hands had been miming all along. Not death. Not exit. But this: the wish to be held. To hold. To press something to my body hard enough to prove the body still existed, still could be marked, still mattered enough to bleed.

I knelt. I took your hands, the ones full of nothing, and I brought them to my throat where the invisible blade had traveled a hundred times. I placed them there. Warm. Living. Trembling.

"Don't mime it," you whispered. "Don't. Just—stay. Stay in the air with me."

Outside, her swing moved. The seed heads shook loose their small inheritances. The whole decaying garden breathed, and for one held moment we breathed with it—two people made of grief and habit, giving each other the only wealth we had left.

Nothing.

Everything.

Air.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an avant-garde prose poem exploring themes of despair, performance, and love, ending with the image of a shadow as the chalk outline of a woman who did not jump.
counterfactuals.output:
# What the Body Leaves

I have rehearsed my dying so many times the stage remembers me kindly, applauds before I fall. There is a craft to it—the tremor calibrated, the held breath sold to the back rows where they pay most for the least. Despair is the only honest theater. Everything else is love pretending it knows the lines.

Watch how I am generous. I give you the wound already dressed, the grief already grieved, the flower pressed flat in a book you'll never open. This is performance: to offer the ghost of feeling so you need not touch the animal beneath, still warm, still asking.

*Do you love me* is a question I have learned to mouth without sound, the way fish practice drowning in the wrong direction. And you—you are so good at watching. You clap at all the right silences.

Here is a confession I keep folding smaller: I wanted to be seen so badly I forgot to be *here.* I built a woman out of witnessed things and left the real one starving in the wings, gnawing on the rope that lowers curtains.

But listen. Somewhere the mechanism failed. Some Tuesday, gray as a swallowed pill, I did not do the thing my body had memorized. I stood at the edge that is every window, every hour, every held breath—and I stepped back into the dull magnificent ache of staying.

No one saw. That is the secret of survival: it has no audience. It happens in the ordinary dark where love, if it is love, arrives without a spotlight, offering only bread, only water, only *stay, stay, stay.*

And now the afternoon lays me down against the wall the way light does, casual, uninsistent. I have become my own outline. Not the fallen woman the story wanted—

but the shadow she cast standing still: the chalk around a body that refused, the perfect drawn absence of the leap I did not take, the woman-shaped survival the sun keeps sketching, erasing, sketching again, saying *look—here is where she lived.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
